In mathematics, [[George Glauberman]]'s '''Z* theorem''' is stated as follows:

<blockquote> '''Z* theorem:''' Let ''G'' be a [[finite group]], with ''O''(''G'') being its maximal [[normal subgroup]] of [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] [[order (group theory)|order]].  If ''T'' is a [[Sylow subgroup|Sylow 2-subgroup]] of ''G'' containing an [[Involution_(mathematics)#Group_theory|involution]] not [[conjugacy class|conjugate]] in ''G'' to any other element of ''T'', then the involution lies in ''Z*''(''G''), which is the inverse image in ''G'' of the [[center (group theory)|center]] of ''G''/''O''(''G'').</blockquote>

This generalizes the [[Brauer–Suzuki theorem]] (and the proof uses the Brauer–Suzuki theorem to deal with some small cases).

==Details==
The original paper {{harvtxt|Glauberman|1966}} gave several criteria for an element to lie outside {{nobreak|''Z*''(''G'').}}  Its theorem 4 states:

<blockquote>For an element ''t'' in ''T'', it is necessary and sufficient for ''t'' to lie outside ''Z*''(''G'') that there is some ''g'' in ''G'' and [[abelian group|abelian subgroup]] ''U'' of ''T'' satisfying the following properties:
# ''g'' normalizes both ''U'' and the [[centralizer]] ''C<sub>T</sub>''(''U''), that is ''g'' is contained in ''N'' = ''N<sub>G</sub>''(''U'') ∩ ''N<sub>G</sub>''(''C<sub>T</sub>''(''U''))
# ''t'' is contained in ''U'' and ''tg'' ≠ ''gt''
# ''U'' is generated by the ''N''-conjugates of ''t''
# the [[exponent (group theory)|exponent]] of ''U'' is equal to the [[order (group theory)|order]] of ''t''

Moreover ''g'' may be chosen to have [[prime power]] order if ''t'' is in the center of ''T'', and ''g'' may be chosen in ''T'' otherwise.</blockquote>

A simple corollary is that an element ''t'' in ''T'' is not in ''Z*''(''G'') if and only if there is some ''s'' ≠ ''t'' such that ''s'' and ''t'' commute and ''s'' and ''t'' are ''G''-conjugate.

A generalization to odd [[prime number|primes]] was recorded in {{harvtxt|Guralnick|Robinson|1993}}: if ''t'' is an element of prime order ''p'' and the [[commutator]] [''t'', ''g''] has order [[coprime]] to ''p'' for all ''g'', then ''t'' is central modulo the [[p-core|''p''′-core]].  This was also generalized to odd primes and to [[compact Lie group]]s in {{harvtxt|Mislin|Thévenaz|1991}}, which also contains several useful results in the finite case.

{{harvtxt|Henke|Semeraro|2015}} have also studied an extension of the Z* theorem to pairs of groups (''G'', ''H'') with ''H'' a normal subgroup of ''G''.
